title: A Visit to the Library
cardDescription: Browse a library through familiar words for shelves, borrowing, book information, and the people who help readers.
description: Browse a library through familiar words for shelves, borrowing, book information, and the people who help readers.
focus: The clues describe library places, records, and lending actions. Some answers name objects or people; others describe what a reader does with a borrowed book.
solvingTip: Check whether a clue asks for a person, a record, a location, or a lending action. Short borrowing words can help cross longer library terms.
words: Place where books are kept for reading or borrowing
Person who helps readers find and use library materials
Horizontal support holding a row of books
Organized list of books and other library items
Small identification item used to borrow library books
Temporary lending of a library item
To take out a book with permission to return it later
To bring a borrowed library item back
To extend the borrowing period of a library book
Required to be returned by a specified date
Request to reserve a library item for later borrowing
Pile or arranged collection of books
Passage between rows of library shelves
Service counter where a reader can ask for help
Person using or enjoying written material
Name under which a book is listed
Alphabetical guide to topics in a book
Collection preserving records or historical documents
One book in a set or series

answerNotes.CATALOG: Catalog lists and describes library items. This is the common American spelling; catalogue is another accepted form.
answerNotes.RENEW: Renew means extend the borrowing period here. It does not mean replacing the book with a new copy.
answerNotes.HOLD: A hold reserves an item for a reader. The word names a request rather than physically gripping a book.
answerNotes.DUE: Due describes the required return date. It sounds like dew, but the lending context determines the spelling.
answerNotes.ARCHIVE: An archive preserves records or historical materials. The word can name a collection rather than just one book.
answerNotes.VOLUME: Volume means one physical book here. The same spelling can describe sound level in another setting.

title: From Cover to Last Page
cardDescription: Open a book through familiar words for its outside, printed pages, and the guides that help readers find information.
description: Open a book through familiar words for its outside, printed pages, and the guides that help readers find information.
focus: This puzzle moves between the physical book and the features of its text. Clues identify an item by its position or purpose, such as an outside covering or a guide near the end.
solvingTip: Look for whether the clue points to the outside, a page feature, or a guide to the text. Edge and end locations can help separate similar book terms.
words: Outer protective surface of a book
Bound edge of a book visible when it stands on a shelf
One side of a sheet in a book
One sheet of a book, with a page on each side
Major numbered or titled division of a book
Name printed on a book's opening display page
Person credited with writing the text
Introductory remarks placed before the main text
List of a book's sections and their starting pages
Alphabetical topic list with page references near a book's end
List explaining specialized words used in a book
Blank space around the edges of a printed page
Explanatory note printed at the bottom of a page
Structure holding a book's pages together
Removable paper covering around a hardcover book
Short promotional description printed on a book's cover
Particular published version of a book
Letters or words produced on paper
Main written words of a book
Thin material on which a book's words are printed

answerNotes.SPINE: Spine names the bound book edge here. It does not refer to the backbone inside a person or animal.
answerNotes.LEAF: A leaf is one sheet with two page surfaces. Page identifies one side, so the two words count different units.
answerNotes.GLOSSARY: A glossary explains words. An index instead points readers to pages where topics occur.
answerNotes.FOOTNOTE: A footnote sits at the foot, or bottom, of a page. The location distinguishes it from a note collected at the book's end.
answerNotes.JACKET: A book jacket is a removable outer paper covering. It is separate from the book's fixed cover and binding.
answerNotes.EDITION: Edition identifies a published version. A changed or revised text can appear in a new edition.

title: Inside a Familiar Story
cardDescription: Explore stories through familiar words for characters, events, narrative forms, and the voice telling the tale.
description: Explore stories through familiar words for characters, events, narrative forms, and the voice telling the tale.
focus: The clues distinguish a whole type of story from an element within one. Characters, events, places, and narrative devices have their own names. No particular novel or author is required.
solvingTip: Check whether the clue names a story form, a character, a place, or a narrative feature. Short tale and action words can help cross longer storytelling terms.
words: Long fictional story usually written in prose
Connected sequence of events in a story
Story section centered on one event or situation
Female leading character admired for brave actions
Story character associated with harmful or opposing actions
Detail that helps explain a story's puzzle
Story built around solving an unexplained event
Writing about imagined characters or events
Short teaching story often featuring talking animals
Lesson drawn from a fable or story
Traditional story associated with a culture's beliefs or origins
Traditional tale associated with a remembered person or place
A story's purposeful search or journey
Another word for a narrated story
Voice or person telling a story
Time and place in which a story happens
Unexpected change in a story's direction

answerNotes.NARRATOR: The narrator tells the story. The author writes it, and the two need not be the same person or voice.
answerNotes.SETTING: Setting identifies the story's time and place. Plot identifies what happens within that setting.
answerNotes.FABLE: A fable often uses animals to present a lesson. The lesson itself is the moral rather than the whole story.
answerNotes.DIALOGUE: Dialogue is conversation between characters. It differs from descriptive narration about their surroundings.
answerNotes.TWIST: A plot twist changes expectations. The clue uses twist for a narrative turn rather than a physical winding motion.
answerNotes.FICTION: Fiction presents imagined events or characters. A fictional story can still draw on real places or historical circumstances.

title: The Sound of a Poem
cardDescription: Enjoy familiar poetry vocabulary for lines, sounds, images, and recognizable poetic forms.
description: Enjoy familiar poetry vocabulary for lines, sounds, images, and recognizable poetic forms.
focus: This puzzle introduces poetry through direct definitions. Some clues name a form; others describe sound patterns, a group of lines, or a way language creates an image. Poems do not all use the same pattern.
solvingTip: Ask whether a clue names a whole form, one unit, or a sound feature. Short reading and sound words can help cross the longer poetic terms.
words: Literary work often arranged in lines for expressive effect
Similarity of ending sounds in words
Pattern of movement or flow in spoken language
One horizontal unit of words in a poem
Grouped set of lines within a poem
Poetic form traditionally made of fourteen lines
Poem of praise or serious reflection
Short Japanese poetic form often presented in three lines in English
Regular pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables
A recurring pulse heard in a spoken poem
Single meaningful unit used in a poem
Sensory picture suggested by descriptive language
Comparison commonly introduced by like or as
Figure describing one thing as another for comparison
To say a word or line again
What is heard when a poem is spoken aloud
To take meaning from written poetic words
To speak a poem aloud, often from memory

answerNotes.STANZA: A stanza groups lines in a poem. It is a larger unit than one line, rather like a verse paragraph.
answerNotes.SONNET: A traditional sonnet has fourteen lines. Different sonnet forms organize rhyme and rhythm in different ways.
answerNotes.HAIKU: Haiku comes from a Japanese poetic tradition. English presentations often use three lines, but not every English haiku follows one fixed syllable count.
answerNotes.SIMILE: A simile commonly uses like or as to make a comparison. A metaphor can state the comparison directly instead.
answerNotes.METER: Meter is an organized stress pattern. Rhythm is the broader movement of language and need not follow a regular metrical scheme.
answerNotes.RHYME: Rhyme concerns matching sounds rather than matching spellings. Poetry can also use free verse without a regular rhyme pattern.

title: A Quiet Reading Corner
cardDescription: Settle into a reading corner with familiar furniture, useful objects, and simple words for enjoying a book.
description: Settle into a reading corner with familiar furniture, useful objects, and simple words for enjoying a book.
focus: The clues describe the small setting around a reader. Some answers name furniture or lighting parts, while others name reading objects or everyday actions.
solvingTip: Look for a whole object, one small part, or an action. A marker left in a book and a protective container for glasses have different names. Short reading words can help with longer objects.
words: Comfortable seat with supports for both arms
Soft pad placed on a reading chair
Movable light beside a reader's seat
Cover around a lamp that directs or softens its light
Replaceable light source inside many reading lamps
Flat-topped furniture holding a book beside a chair
Strip or object left between pages to mark one's place
Pair of lenses worn to help with seeing
Protective container used to store reading spectacles
Horizontal board where books are stored
Bound collection of pages for reading
One printed side turned while reading
To move from one book page to the next
To follow and understand written words
To take a break in a comfortable chair
Having little noise around a reading place
Place where two walls meet, used for a reading nook
Small blanket draped over a chair
Handled cup placed beside a reader
Device showing the time near a reading chair

answerNotes.BOOKMARK: A bookmark marks the reader's place between pages. It is separate from the printed page itself.
answerNotes.SHADE: Shade names a lamp covering here. It differs from shade outdoors, though both meanings relate to controlling light.
answerNotes.BULB: Bulb means a lighting part in this clue. It is not the underground storage structure of a plant.
answerNotes.THROW: Throw is a noun for a small blanket here. The clue does not ask for the action of tossing something.
answerNotes.GLASSES: Glasses is a plural-form word for a pair of lenses and their frame. The clue describes spectacles rather than drinking vessels.
answerNotes.CASE: Case means a protective container. The reading-spectacles context distinguishes it from a legal matter or a grammatical category.
